name: Quercitrin

lead: Quercitrin is a flavonoid found in buckwheat, oak and some herbal extracts. It is discussed as a possible hair-supportive plant compound because of its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies.
No published human trial has tested it for hair growth, so its appearance benefit is unproven.

paras: In animal and cell studies it is broken down to quercetin and dampens inflammatory signalling such as NF-kappaB and iNOS. None of this has been shown in hair follicles.
Safety for hair use has not been studied. Dietary exposure through plant foods is common; concentrated topical or supplement use has no published hair-related safety data.

lead: Quercitrin (quercetin 3-rhamnoside, also called thujin) is a flavonoid glycoside in which the flavonol quercetin is bound to the sugar rhamnose [1]. It occurs in plants such as Tartary buckwheat and several oak species, and in the dye quercitron [1][2].

It is listed in hair-care discussions as a plant flavonoid with possible hair-growth relevance. Published research on quercitrin itself concerns antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cells and animal models, mainly in the gut and in immune cells [3][4]. No published human study has tested quercitrin for hair growth or hair loss.
infobox: Tartary buckwheat, oak species, St John's wort extracts [1][2]

paras: Quercitrin has a molar mass of about 448 g/mol. The enzyme quercitrinase hydrolyses it to L-rhamnose and quercetin [1]. Tartary buckwheat herb contains quercitrin at roughly 0.01 to 0.05 percent of dry weight, alongside much larger amounts of rutin [2]. Quercitrin is also one of the flavonoids reported in extracts of Hypericum perforatum [5].
Human gut bacteria can cleave flavonoid glycosides such as quercitrin to release the aglycone quercetin, a step reported in early work on intestinal Bacteroides strains [6].

In a mouse model of intestinal inflammation, researchers found that the anti-inflammatory effect of quercitrin involved release of quercetin and down-regulation of the NF-kappaB pathway [3]. A related study associated quercitrin's effect with reduced iNOS expression [7]. In a cell-culture study, quercetin and quercitrin both reduced inflammatory and oxidative markers in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophage-like cells [4].

These findings are not hair-specific. Inflammation and oxidative stress are themes in some hair-loss research, which is the reason given for interest in flavonoids generally, but no source reviewed here links quercitrin to hair follicles.
Related laboratory and animal work on quercitrin and quercetin addresses inflammation and antioxidant activity, not hair [3][4][7].
